title: Joshua 19:40–48
context: The seventh and last lot falls to Dan, whose towns lie to the west of Benjamin and Judah, including Zorah, Eshtaol, Timnah and Ekron, names later tied to Samson’s story (Judges 13:2, 25; 14:1). The allotment also notes that Dan’s border went beyond these towns, because the Danites fought against Leshem, took it, and renamed it Dan. Leshem is commonly identified with the Laish of Judges 18, which tells a fuller and less flattering account of that migration after Dan struggled to hold its first allotment (Judges 1:34). Arminian and Reformed readers commonly read this passage as shared ground about the gift of land and the difficulties of possessing it. They generally avoid building doctrine on the Danite migration, which Judges presents critically.

verses.text: The seventh lot came out for the tribe of the children of Dan according to their families.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the seventh and last lot comes out for Dan according to their families. Every tribe, including the last, receives its portion from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the final lot as completing God’s orderly distribution among the tribes. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a reminder that no tribe was forgotten.

verses.text: The border of their inheritance was Zorah, Eshtaol, Irshemesh,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers notice Zorah and Eshtaol, the area later linked with Samson’s family (Judges 13:2, 25). The allotment prepares the setting for later stories of God’s deliverance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence in the places assigned to Dan, where he would later raise up a deliverer. Readers in both traditions commonly find meaning in these connections without pressing them too far.

verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Shaalabbin, Aijalon and Ithlah as part of Dan’s initial inheritance. These towns lay in a region that Dan would struggle to hold (compare Judges 1:34).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the listing as a faithful record of what God assigned. Both traditions commonly note that the gap between allotment and possession is a recurring theme in Joshua and Judges.

verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers notice Timnah and Ekron, towns later associated with the Philistines. Dan’s inheritance bordered powerful neighbors who would challenge its hold on the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inclusion of these towns as showing the full extent of what God promised. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as describing allotment rather than secure possession at that time.

verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Eltekeh, Gibbethon and Baalath as further towns in Dan’s portion. Each name is part of the concrete fulfillment of God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list continuing as testimony to the detail of God’s provision. The locations of some of these towns are uncertain, and readers in both traditions commonly hold them with caution.

verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Jehud, Bene Berak and Gath Rimmon as part of Dan’s territory. These towns filled out the inheritance toward the coastal plain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the specific listing as reflecting God’s careful allotment. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the shared testimony to God’s faithfulness in giving land.

verses.text: Me Jarkon, and Rakkon, with the border opposite Joppa.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers notice that the border lay opposite Joppa, giving Dan an inheritance reaching toward the sea. God’s gift extended to the coast.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the coastal border as completing the description of Dan’s first allotment. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse without drawing doctrinal conclusions from it.

verses.text: The border of the children of Dan went out beyond them; for the children of Dan went up and fought against Leshem, and took it, and struck it with the edge of the sword, and possessed it, and lived therein, and called Leshem, Dan, after the name of Dan their forefather.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Danites going beyond their first allotment, taking Leshem and renaming it Dan, as a response to the difficulty of holding their original land. Judges 18 tells this story more fully and critically.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Leshem is commonly identified with Laish in Judges 18:29, where the conquest is narrated in a way that exposes the tribe’s failings. Both traditions commonly read this verse as a brief note rather than an endorsement of everything Judges later describes.

verses.text: This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Dan according to their families, these cities with their villages.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the closing formula confirming Dan’s inheritance by families. Even a tribe that struggled is still named as having received its portion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the summary as affirming God’s faithfulness to Dan despite the tribe’s later difficulties. Readers in both traditions commonly find hope in God’s commitment to give each tribe a place.
